deep.reconstruction: Setting (from the surrounding pages): Σ = {Δ_i}_{i∈I} is a system of n pseudo-lines in the real projective plane X. Γ(Σ) is a graph whose vertices Pr(Σ) are pseudo-lines D taken up to isotopy relative to Σ, with 'specialization' arrows D→D' given by pushing D across a crossing. For each D, Pol(D) is the combinatorial polygon cut out on D by the Δ_i. Here D̃ is the double (orientation) cover, a circle. Its 'blown-up' version P̂(D) has its vertices and edges indexed by Ĩ, the set of 2n oriented pseudo-lines, compatibly with the antipodal involution. This page treats the 'super-critical' case D = Δ_{i0}, where D is itself one of the lines of Σ. Each vertex of Δ_{i0} is split into as many vertices as there are other lines through it (its weight). Equivalently, one reads off the order of the points cut by the Δ_i (i ≠ i0) on a nearby parallel pushed to one side of Δ_{i0}. This gives a combinatorial polygon P̂(Δ_{i0}) of order 2(n−1). It comes with a canonical bijection between its vertices and the oriented versions of the Δ_i, i ≠ i0, compatible with the antipodisms. The marginal NB says this bijection depends on a chosen orientation of Δ_{i0}; reversing the orientation composes it with the antipodism. The two figures show a zigzag (grey) perturbation and a green curve D, close to Δ_{i0}, that changes sides at a multiple point. They illustrate that the one-sided 'modified' parallel and an ordinary transversal give comparable data. The count ν + ν0 = n relates the two: ν0 is a number of directed edges / one-sided crossings, and the complementary count is n − ν. So the 'modified perpendicular' is determined by the ordinary one, and conversely all such data near D are recovered by local formulas. Grothendieck then states a global result. There is a canonical map from Pr(Σ) ∪ Σ (vertices of Γ(Σ) together with the critical pseudo-lines Δ_i) to the set of 'polygonal structures' on Ĩ compatible with the antipodism. He expects this map to be injective without difficulty. He lists two follow-up tasks: (1) follow P(Δ), P̂(Δ) along specialization arrows (begun on the next page as a local mutation rule), and (2) interpret the whole oriented-graph structure (alternating polygons, orientations of edges and corners) in terms of these polygonal structures. In modern terms: Σ is a rank-3 oriented matroid M on I. A pseudo-line D in general position is a single-element extension M ∪ d. An antipodally compatible polygonal structure on Ĩ is exactly a rank-2 (uniform) oriented matroid on I, i.e. a signed cyclic order. The map D ↦ P̂(D) is the contraction (M ∪ d)/d. For D = Δ_{i0} it is the contraction M/i0, made uniform by a one-sided perturbation. That perturbation is a lexicographic-type extension placed next to i0, which is why the orientation choice enters. Injectivity holds: χ_{M∪d}(d,i,j) = χ_{(M∪d)/d}(i,j), and M ∪ d is determined by M together with these values. Γ(Σ) with its specialization arrows is essentially the extension space / mutation graph of M. Moving D across a vertex changes the cyclic order by a local reversal, as in Goodman–Pollack allowable sequences.
errors: The bijection is written 'I∖{i} ≃ sommets de P̂(Δ_{i0})'. Since P̂(Δ_{i0}) has 2(n−1) vertices, the domain must be the oriented index set Ĩ minus the two orientations of i0 (equivalently Ĩ∖{±i0}), not the (n−1)-element set I∖{i0}. This is likely a slip or a transcription loss of the tilde.

The injectivity of Pr(Σ) ∪ Σ → {antipodal polygonal structures on Ĩ} is asserted without proof ('ne devrait pas être difficile'). It is true in the generic case via the chirotope argument. For the critical members Δ_i, one must check that the one-sided perturbation does not produce collisions with polygons coming from generic D. Plausibly it does not, since the polygon has order 2(n−1) rather than 2n, but this is unstated.
The meaning of ν, ν0 and of 'perpendiculaire' is only partly legible. The relation ν + ν0 = n is stated without derivation on this page.

ideas.what: One-sided perturbation of a line of the arrangement to obtain a generic polygon of order 2(n−1) on the remaining lines, depending on an orientation choice up to antipodism.
ideas.modern_name: Contraction M/i0 of a rank-3 oriented matroid, made uniform by a lexicographic (one-sided) perturbation/extension
ideas.usually_credited_to: Las Vergnas; Bland–Las Vergnas (late 1970s); perturbation techniques in oriented matroid theory (Björner–Las Vergnas–Sturmfels–White–Ziegler book, 1993)

ideas.what: Map from isotopy classes of pseudo-lines relative to Σ (plus the lines of Σ) to signed antipodal cyclic orders on Ĩ, claimed injective.
ideas.modern_name: Single-element extension determined by its contraction (localization/chirotope of M∪d versus M/d); local sequences
ideas.usually_credited_to: Las Vergnas (single-element extensions, 1978); Goodman–Pollack (local sequences / allowable sequences, 1980–84)

ideas.what: Graph Γ(Σ) of pseudo-lines with specialization arrows; program to track the polygons along arrows and to read the graph's alternating-polygon structure in terms of polygonal structures on Ĩ.
ideas.modern_name: Extension space / mutation graph of a rank-3 oriented matroid; cyclic order changes under mutations (allowable sequences)
ideas.where_published: Pseudo-line configurations are mentioned only allusively in Grothendieck's reflective writings, if at all; unsure

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets out a program to describe the whole oriented graph Γ(Σ) — alternating polygons, orientations of edges and corners — purely in terms of antipodal cyclic orders on Ĩ. This amounts to a combinatorial description of the extension space of a rank-3 oriented matroid via contractions. The program is stated but not carried out here.
missed.quote: Il faudrait de plus, pour bien faire, voir : 1) Comment "suivre" les P(Δ), P̂(Δ) le long d'une flèche de spécialisation
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Extension spaces of rank-3 oriented matroids are well studied (they are known to be connected; the general extension space conjecture was disproved in higher rank by Mnëv–Ziegler/Liu). A description by local rules on cyclic orders is close to known allowable-sequence techniques. So this is at most a mild historical curiosity, an independent rediscovery.

deep.surprise_reason: The page independently rediscovers, in Grothendieck's own language, standard rank-3 oriented-matroid facts: contraction, one-sided perturbation, and an extension being determined by its contraction. These were known by 1983 (Folkman–Lawrence, Las Vergnas, Goodman–Pollack). It is of historical interest as evidence of Grothendieck's combinatorial work, but contains nothing new to specialists.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'on extrait des sommets que l'indique' is more likely 'on éclate les sommets en autant que l'indiquent les poids' (blowing up vertices according to their weights), consistent with the previous page.
'I∖{i} ≃' should read Ĩ∖{i0} (oriented index set minus i0); the image shows a mark over I and the subscript i0 is lost.
'(i≠i0)' and 'parallèle à Δ' are correct; the image shows 'Δ_i (i≠i_0) sur une parallèle à Δ'.
The right-column formula reads 'ν + ν0 = n', preceded by 'd'où'.
'p.s. supposé critique' under Σ is better read 'p.-d. supposées critiques' (pseudo-droites supposées critiques).
The target set reads 'ens. des structures polygonales sur Ĩ compatibles avec l'antipodisme'.
